title: Rendering of reference and pointer parameters in markdown script
body:
Currently a parameter with a ref or pointer renders with a space after the ref like this: `Device & somedevice` or `Device * somedevice` (rendering is fine value parameters).

The question is, should this render as `Device& somedevice` or `Device &somedevice`

(as an aside, the second format is slightly harder, because for pointers, care needs to be taken to make sure the * is not interpreted as "make text italic".

This originates here: https://github.com/dronecore/docs/pull/107#discussion_r174682278

comments.body: Which is best is a matter of style - have we standardized on this in source code?

This has been set with #410 in:

https://github.com/dronecore/DroneCore/blob/develop/.clang-format#L55 

to `Device &somedevice`.

There are [pros and cons](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/398395/why-is-the-asterisk-before-the-variable-name-rather-than-after-the-type), however, the [CppCoreGuidelines](https://github.com/isocpp/CppCoreGuidelines/blob/master/CppCoreGuidelines.md#nl18-use-c-style-declarator-layout ) suggest to use `Device& somedevice`.

Given that I would suggest we switch it. It's as easy as changing `.clang-format` and doing `make fix_style`.

@julianoes In above, `Device &somedevice` = `Device &somedevice` :-)

Whatever alignment is used is fine as long as we're consistent.
@hamishwillee thanks fixed above.
We should change it to `Device& somedevice` according to [CppCoreGuidelines](https://github.com/isocpp/CppCoreGuidelines/blob/master/CppCoreGuidelines.md#nl18-use-c-style-declarator-layout).

title: Add option to build without curl
body: For slow compilation (e.g. on embedded boards) it would be nice to be able to build without curl.

comments.body: Isn't it good enough to cross-compile for those boards? If we make it optional in the code, we will also need to make it optional in the superbuild (because I guess we don't expect people to figure out that by themselves), and that adds complexity and corner cases everywhere...
Sometimes you're in a debugging situation where you just need to rebuild on the device.

Right. But I don't think that adding options in CMakeLists and ifdefs in the code is the right solution for debugging on the device.

If you are debugging curl on the device, then you need to compile it. If you are debugging MAVSDK, then you don't have to recompile curl. Yes, that implies that you may need to not use our superbuild and to learn how to do that (e.g. cross-compile the dependencies separately, copy that on your device and build mavsdk on the device without SUPERBUILD=ON). But that's "basic" dependency management in cmake. I'm happy to write a superbuild to make that easier for most use-cases, but for specific use-cases, I believe that developers should learn how to deal with that.

To me it would be the same as saying "we should make it such that cmake checks if the submodules are correctly synced, because we don't want our developers to have to know about git submodules", and then "cmake should show a warning when people push to their fork without having an 'upstream' branch, because not everyone knows how to work with a fork".

We can do all that, but it results in more code that we need to maintain, and it forces devs to learn about our custom wrappers instead of learning to use the actual tools.

Am I too much of a purist? :laughing:
I agree with your examples but this is more a request that the MAVSDK should be able to build and run with minimal dependencies if required.

For the record: it still requires curl but you can now also use libcurl from the system instead of getting it via git and building it. The way to do so is to use the configure option `cmake -DSUPERBUILD=OFF` for the configure step. Note this is supported as of Ubuntu 18.04 but not 16.04.

comments.body:
For now, `mavsdk_server` does not support multiple drones (i.e. multiple drones running on the same MAVLink port, here 14540). Only MAVSDK-C++ does.

However, you can run multiple instances of `mavsdk_server`, each listenning to a different mavlink port, by using the latest `develop` branch of MAVSDK.

That would be something like:

```sh
./mavsdk_server -p 50040 udp://:14540
./mavsdk_server -p 50041 udp://:14541
./mavsdk_server -p 50042 udp://:14542
```

And then you could instantiate multiple instances of a wrapper. For instance in Python:

```python
from mavsdk import System

...

drone1 = System(mavsdk_server_address="localhost", port=50040)
await drone1.connect()
drone2 = System(mavsdk_server_address="localhost", port=50041)
await drone2.connect()
drone3 = System(mavsdk_server_address="localhost", port=50042)
await drone3.connect()

...
```

And then you could use your drone objects (`drone1`, `drone2` and `drone3` separately):

```
await drone1.action.arm()
await drone2.action.arm()
await drone3.action.arm()
```

## Problem
Currently it seems like we can't arbitrarily set the parameter before booting up, neither can we reboot the vehicle in the SITL test function.

### Proposed Solutions
1. Have a way to reboot the vehicle after setting the parameter in the mavsdk sitl test pipeline
2. Have a way to load an arbitrary / modified parameter through MAVSDK interface for the drone

If we want to support such feature, what would be the best way to implement it? Are there any other solutions? Would this be possible without modifying MAVSDK?

title: Add support for disabling native heartbeat sending and triggering HEARTBEAT over gRPC
body:
I would like to contribute a feature that lets MAVSDK users disable internally generated HEARTBEAT sending and instead trigger transmission through gRPC.

The gRPC API would be a fail-closed, one-shot request to send a single MAVSDK-configured HEARTBEAT, not a toggle or persistent enable state. If the client stops calling, disconnects, or fails, MAVSDK does not continue sending heartbeats through that path. The client is responsible for calling at the desired rate (e.g. ~1 Hz).

The gRPC call would not set HEARTBEAT fields; MAVSDK continues to own message content (sysid, compid, mav_type, etc.). The call only requests that MAVSDK send its configured heartbeat.

Some integrations need an external process to control when MAVSDK sends heartbeats, while MAVSDK still constructs the actual MAVLink HEARTBEAT message. This avoids duplicating heartbeat construction outside MAVSDK.

**Proposed Solution**
- Add a configuration option (e.g. automatic_heartbeats_enabled) to disable native heartbeat sending.
- Add a gRPC API to trigger one configured HEARTBEAT per request.
- Optionally expose via mavsdk_server CLI (e.g. --no-automatic-heartbeats).

Default behavior stays unchanged.

comments.body:
Is your use-case that you want MAVSDK to stop sending heartbeats in case your program crashes? If it is something different, can you explain it?

Also you mention gRPC so I assume you are using some MAVSDK bindings. Which ones? MAVSDK-Python?

Yes, that is the main use case.

We are using MAVSDK to interface with a PX4 vehicle from our own application. We want the heartbeat to represent the health/presence of the application using MAVSDK, not just whether MAVSDK-server is still running.

If that application crashes, disconnects from MAVSDK-server, or stops servicing the control path, we want PX4 to see the GCS/companion component as offline so it can trigger the configured MAVLink lost-link failsafe behavior, such as RTL.

We also have test cases where we want to continue subscribing to telemetry from PX4 through MAVSDK, while intentionally disabling outbound heartbeat transmission so we can verify PX4's lost-link behavior.

We are not using MAVSDK-Python. We are using our own application that communicates with MAVSDK-server over gRPC.
I guess that would be acceptable as a feature. What do you think @JonasVautherin? Either explicit heartbeat triggering, or a timeout that stops it?
I like the timeout idea as long as it can be configured at runtime.
Yeah I think it should work 👍

Thanks @JonasVautherin 

Following the timeout idea @julianoes suggested, I’m planning to implement this as a heartbeat watchdog (deadman timer) rather than the original one-shot “send one HEARTBEAT per gRPC call” design.

The idea is that MAVSDK keeps sending periodic heartbeats as it does today and still owns the message content (sysid, compid, mav_type, etc.). The client’s job is to keep feeding the watchdog over gRPC at roughly the desired rate. If the client crashes, hangs, or disconnects and stops feeding, heartbeats stop after the configured timeout so PX4 can treat the GCS/companion as offline and trigger lost-link failsafes like RTL.

The timeout would be configurable at runtime, and default behavior would stay unchanged when the watchdog isn’t enabled. That should cover both our production use case (heartbeats reflect application liveness, not just mavsdk_server) and our lost-link testing (subscribe to telemetry, stop feeding, verify failsafe behavior).

Let me know if that direction works for you and I’ll open a PR.
Yes that works for me 👍
